extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and working stand-up comedians / comedy performers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on employing act-outs, impressions, and physicality in stand-up to get laughs, including when to use them, how to shape them, and common pitfalls. Focused on performance technique rather than writing structure or business aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act-out (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Act-out: stand-up jargon describing a comic’s shift from narrating a joke to acting it. Dramatizing a conversation, for instance, or impersonating an animal, vegetable or anatomical part are examples of act-outs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act-outs turn description into dramatized dialogue and behavior — showing instead of telling — and can include impressions, impersonations, or simply doing the lines rather than summarizing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of thumb: act out struggling punchlines
rubrics_metrics.description: If a joke’s not getting a laugh, act out the punchline somehow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an act-out to salvage or sharpen a joke; audiences love impressions and seeing someone pretend to be someone (or something) else, so dramatizing a punchline can generate laughs where narration fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use impressions but beware of offense
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences love to see impressions, but be mindful of what you imitate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An impression can be effective, but avoid racist or appropriative accents (example: 'if you’re, say, a white dude, maybe don’t break out the Chinese accent when you’re doing an act out about going to the laundromat'). Consider the social cost and audience reaction before adopting cultural or ethnic stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: You don’t have to be a great actor
rubrics_metrics.description: You don’t actually have to be a great actor or do a perfect impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivering a line in your own voice can still get solid laughs; sometimes getting it wrong intentionally or awkwardly is part of the humor. Don’t let lack of acting ability stop you from using act-outs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don’t tell — specificity wins
rubrics_metrics.description: Act-outs force you to take an abstract concept and put it into lines of dialogue. Both comedy and truth are frequently found in the specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By dramatizing specifics you create 'aha' moments. Use concrete dialogue and moments of behavior to reveal comedy rather than summarizing or analyzing situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and crowd dynamics: bigger crowds benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: The bigger the crowd, the more an act out helps you get over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act-outs can beef up the scale of a joke and make punch lines broader and more emphatic — helpful when you need to reach a large room; they increase clarity and emphasis compared to dry observational analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior over analysis — use act-outs for storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Act-outs make behavior, rather than analysis, the focus; the device can be essential to comedic storytelling, while blurring the lines between stand-up and one-person show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When your comedy relies on demonstrating characters or interactions, prefer act-outs to expository explanation so the audience experiences the scene directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act-outs as embellishment vs centerpiece
rubrics_metrics.description: Most working stand-ups use act-outs to expand and embroider a joke. But a few make them the centerpiece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether act-outs will be occasional amplifiers or the dominant mode of a bit (e.g., Robin Williams and Eddie Murphy built many bits around sustained, motor-mouth act-outs). Match the technique to your persona and material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtle act-outs can be effective
rubrics_metrics.description: Good act-outs can be subtle and flesh out another side of a joke, taking the audience beyond the point of view of the comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don’t always need broad, over-the-top pantomime; restrained or deadpan act-outs (Stephen Wright example) can provide contrast and nuance, enriching the joke without overpowering it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature over on-the-nose imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Make act-outs/caricatures that are 'never quite on the nose' rather than exact replicas of real people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As with Rachel Feinstein’s characters, effective act-outs are caricatures with a distinctive eccentricity — they evoke types without sounding exactly like anyone you’ve heard before. Being slightly off can make them funnier and safer than literal mimicry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicality and treating the stage as movement space
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the stage like a dance floor; use physicality in act-outs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical movement and bodily embodiment enhance act-outs and can convert them into full performance sketches. Use posture, gestures, and spatial dynamics to sell character shifts, but integrate physicality in service of the joke rather than as gratuitous activity.
